topic: RMF structure, Prepare step and roles

notes.front: What is the Prepare step of the Risk Management Framework?
notes.back: Essential activities at organisation, mission and business process, and system levels that ready the organisation to manage security and privacy risk with the RMF.
notes.explanation: Its tasks are split into an organisation-level set and a system-level set.
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Prepare step is to carry out essential activities at the organization, mission and business process, and information system levels of the organization to help prepare the organization to manage its security and privacy risks using the Risk Management Framework.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Prepare (purpose), PDF p. 47
notes.example: Like a hospital agreeing who does what before its first operation, not during it: a ministry names its risk officials and writes its risk strategy before any new system is categorised.

notes.front: What is an authorising official (AO) in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: A senior official or executive with authority to formally assume responsibility and accountability for operating a system, providing inherited controls or using an external service.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 calls the AO the only organisational official who can accept the security and privacy risk to operations, assets and individuals.
notes.evidence: The authorizing official is a senior official or executive with the authority to formally assume responsibility and accountability for operating a system
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official, PDF p. 133
notes.example: Like a pilot-in-command who signs for the aircraft before take-off: the director of a benefits agency signs to say the risk of running its claims system is acceptable.

notes.front: What is an authorising official designated representative (AODR)?
notes.back: An official designated by the AO and empowered to coordinate and conduct day-to-day risk management activities on the AO's behalf.
notes.explanation: This includes carrying out many of the activities in executing the RMF.
notes.evidence: The authorizing official designated representative is an organizational official designated by the authorizing official who is empowered to act on behalf of the authorizing official to coordinate and conduct the day-to-day activities
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official designated representative, PDF p. 134
notes.example: Like a deputy head teacher who runs the timetable but cannot sign the school's accounts: the AO's deputy chases assessment evidence all year.

notes.front: What is a common control provider (CCP) in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: An individual, group or organisation responsible for implementing, assessing and monitoring controls that organisational systems inherit.
notes.explanation: Organisations can have several providers, depending on how security and privacy responsibilities are allocated.
notes.evidence: The common control provider is an individual, group, or organization that is responsible for the implementation, assessment, and monitoring of common controls (i.e., controls inherited by organizational systems).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Common control provider, PDF p. 135
notes.example: Like a landlord who maintains the building's fire alarms for every tenant: a facilities team runs the badge-entry system that every application in the data centre relies on.

notes.front: What is a control assessor in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: An individual, group or organisation that comprehensively assesses implemented controls to determine their effectiveness.
notes.explanation: Effectiveness means the controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome.
notes.evidence: The control assessor is an individual, group, or organization responsible for conducting a comprehensive assessment of implemented controls and control enhancements to determine the effectiveness of the controls
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Control assessor, PDF p. 136
notes.example: Like a building inspector who checks the wiring actually works, not just that it was installed: a team tests whether a bank's log reviews really happen weekly.

notes.front: What is the chief information officer (CIO) responsible for, in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: Designating a senior agency information security officer; maintaining security policies and procedures; reporting to the agency head on the security programme's effectiveness.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 also gives the CIO oversight of personnel with significant security responsibilities, including their training.
notes.evidence: The chief information officer 117 is an organizational official responsible for designating a senior agency information security officer; developing and maintaining security policies, procedures, and control techniques to address security requirements
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Chief information officer, PDF p. 134
notes.example: Like a chief engineer who appoints a safety lead and reports to the board: a council's head of information technology appoints its security chief and reports on the programme each year.

notes.front: What is the senior agency information security officer (SAISO)?
notes.back: The official who carries out the chief information officer's security responsibilities and is the CIO's primary liaison to AOs, system owners and others.
notes.explanation: Organisations may also call this role the senior information security officer or chief information security officer.
notes.evidence: The senior agency information security officer is an organizational official responsible for carrying out the chief information officer security responsibilities
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior agency information security officer, PDF p. 141
notes.example: Like a company's head of health and safety reporting to the operations director: the agency's chief information security officer runs the security programme for the CIO.

notes.front: What is the senior agency official for privacy (SAOP)?
notes.back: The senior official with agency-wide responsibility and accountability for complying with privacy requirements and managing privacy risk.
notes.explanation: The role is the privacy counterpart that the SAISO coordinates with.
notes.evidence: The senior agency official for privacy is the senior official or executive with agency-wide responsibility and accountability for ensuring compliance with applicable privacy requirements and managing privacy risk.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior agency official for privacy, PDF p. 141
notes.example: Like a hospital's Caldicott guardian for patient data, but agency-wide: one official answers for how every department handles personal records.

notes.front: Who is the senior accountable official for risk management?
notes.back: The individual who leads the risk executive (function) and aligns security and privacy risk management with strategic, operational and budgetary planning.
notes.explanation: It is the head of the agency or someone the head designates.
notes.evidence: The senior accountable official for risk management is the individual that leads and manages the risk executive (function) in an organization and is responsible for aligning information security and privacy risk management processes with strategic, operational, and budgetary planning processes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior accountable official for risk management, PDF p. 140
uses: senior accountable official for risk management
introduces: senior accountable official for risk management
notes.example: Like a chief risk officer who chairs a bank's risk board: a deputy secretary chairs the department's risk committee and ties its decisions to the budget.

notes.front: Who is the system owner in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: The official responsible for the procurement, development, integration, modification, operation, maintenance and disposal of a system.
notes.explanation: Organisations may call system owners program managers or business or asset owners.
notes.evidence: The system owner is an organizational official responsible for the procurement, development, integration, modification, operation, maintenance, and disposal of a system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System owner, PDF p. 142
notes.example: Like the owner of a car who buys, services and finally scraps it: the manager of a payroll programme answers for the payroll system from purchase to retirement.

notes.front: Who is the information owner or steward in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: The official with statutory, management or operational authority for specified information, who sets the policies for its generation, collection, processing, dissemination and disposal.
notes.explanation: The information owner may or may not be the same person as the system owner.
notes.evidence: The information owner or steward is an organizational official with statutory, management, or operational authority for specified information and the responsibility for establishing the policies and procedures governing its generation, collection, processing, dissemination, and disposal.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Information owner or steward, PDF p. 138
notes.example: Like a librarian who decides who may borrow rare books, whatever building they sit in: the registrar sets the rules for student records held in several systems.

notes.front: What is the system security officer (SSO) in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: The individual responsible for ensuring the security posture of a system is maintained, working closely with the system owner.
notes.explanation: In many organisations the SSO also handles day-to-day system security operations.
notes.evidence: The system security or privacy officer 124 is an individual responsible for ensuring that the security and privacy posture is maintained for an organizational system and works in close collaboration with the system owner.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System security or privacy officer, PDF p. 143
notes.example: Like a ship's engineer who keeps the engines running for the captain: the security officer for a tax portal watches its logs and handles its incidents day to day.

notes.front: Who is the mission or business owner in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: The senior official with specific mission or line-of-business responsibilities and a security or privacy interest in the systems supporting them.
notes.explanation: Mission or business owners help set the business processes, protection needs and security and privacy requirements.
notes.evidence: The mission or business owner is the senior official or executive within an organization with specific mission or line of business responsibilities and that has a security or privacy interest in the organizational systems supporting those missions or lines of business.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Mission or business owner, PDF p. 138
notes.example: Like the head of a shop floor who needs the tills to work: the director of passport services needs the passport application system to be trustworthy.

notes.front: What is the head of agency responsible and accountable for, in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: Providing information security protections commensurate with the risk to operations, assets, individuals, other organisations and the Nation.
notes.explanation: The head of agency is also the senior official responsible for protecting privacy interests and managing PII responsibly.
notes.evidence: The head of agency is responsible and accountable for providing information security protections commensurate with the risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Head of agency, PDF p. 137
notes.example: Like a ship's owner who answers for the whole fleet: a department secretary answers for how well every system in the department is protected.

notes.front: What is the enterprise architect in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: An individual or group working with leadership and experts to build a holistic view of missions, processes, information and information technology assets.
notes.explanation: For security and privacy, enterprise architects help place systems in the enterprise architecture and serve as part of the risk executive (function).
notes.evidence: The enterprise architect is an individual or group responsible for working with the leadership and subject matter experts in an organization to build a holistic view of the organization's
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Enterprise architect, PDF p. 136
notes.example: Like a town planner who decides where each building goes: an architect maps which of a ministry's systems share data and where a new one should sit.

notes.front: Special Publication 800-37 says the RMF provides a disciplined, structured and {{c1::flexible}} process for managing security and privacy risk.
notes.explanation: The process covers categorisation, control selection, implementation and assessment, authorisations and continuous monitoring.
notes.evidence: The RMF provides a disciplined, structured, and flexible process for managing security and privacy risk
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Abstract, PDF p. 4

notes.front: In Special Publication 800-37, on what determination does the Authorize step rest?
notes.back: That the risk to operations and assets, individuals, other organisations and the Nation is acceptable.
notes.explanation: The step authorises the system or the inherited controls on that basis.
notes.evidence: Authorize the system or common controls based on a determination that the risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation is acceptable.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.2, RMF steps and structure, PDF p. 28

notes.front: Special Publication 800-37 lists the RMF steps in order, but the steps following the Prepare step can be carried out in a {{c1::nonsequential}} order.
notes.explanation: Only the Prepare step has a fixed place at the start.
notes.evidence: the steps following the Prepare step can be carried out in a nonsequential order.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.2, RMF steps and structure, PDF p. 28

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-37, how do organisations running the RMF for the first time for a system typically carry out the remaining steps after Prepare?
notes.back: In sequential order.
notes.explanation: Divergence is still possible, for example for the type of system or iterative cycles between tasks.
notes.evidence: of common controls typically carry out the remaining steps in sequential order.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.2, RMF steps and structure, PDF p. 29

notes.front: Which RMF steps and tasks does Special Publication 800-37 expect organisations to execute?
notes.back: All of them, apart from tasks labelled as optional.
notes.explanation: Organisations still have significant flexibility in how each step and task is carried out.
notes.evidence: Organizations are expected to execute all steps and tasks in the RMF (apart from tasks labeled as optional).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.2, Flexibility in RMF implementation, PDF p. 29

notes.front: A health agency's appointment system has been authorised and is in the Monitor step. A new video-consultation feature is added, changing what the system does. What does Special Publication 800-37 allow?
notes.back: C) Revisiting one or more earlier RMF steps to address the change
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 says changes in risk or system functionality may require revisiting RMF steps, so execution need not stay in order.
notes.evidence: changes in risk or in system functionality may necessitate revisiting one or more of the steps in the RMF to address the change.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.2, RMF steps and structure, PDF p. 29
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: once in Monitor, the steps must never be revisited
B) Starting again from the Prepare step for the whole organisation
C) Revisiting one or more earlier RMF steps to address the change
D) Skipping assessment because the system was already authorised
notes.choicesExplained: A: Special Publication 800-37 expressly allows nonsequential execution once in Monitor. B: organisation-level preparation is not repeated for one system's change. D: the change is exactly what may need reassessing.

notes.front: What does Special Publication 800-37 Revision 2 call the addition of the Prepare step?
notes.back: One of the key changes to the RMF.
notes.explanation: It was added to achieve more effective, efficient and cost-effective security and privacy risk management processes.
notes.evidence: The addition of the Prepare step is one of the key changes to the RMF
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Preface, PDF p. 8

notes.front: Which Prepare step objective does Special Publication 800-37 say reduces the workload on individual system owners?
notes.back: Promoting organisation-wide identification of inherited controls and organisationally tailored control baselines.
notes.explanation: Doing this once for the organisation also cuts the cost of system development and protection.
notes.evidence: Promote organization-wide identification of common controls and the development of organizationally-tailored control baselines, to reduce the workload on individual system owners
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Chapter 3, Organization and system preparation, PDF p. 46

notes.front: Which two organisation-level Prepare tasks does Special Publication 800-37 label as optional?
notes.back: P-4, organisationally tailored control baselines and CSF Profiles; and P-6, impact-level prioritisation.
notes.explanation: Optional tasks give organisations extra options to make their RMF implementations more effective, efficient and cost-effective.
notes.evidence: ORGANIZATIONALLY-TAILORED CONTROL BASELINES AND CYBERSECURITY FRAMEWORK PROFILES (OPTIONAL) COMMON CONTROL IDENTIFICATION IMPACT-LEVEL PRIORITIZATION (OPTIONAL)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Table 1, PDF p. 47

notes.front: In Special Publication 800-37, when a role with primary responsibility delegates an RMF task, who remains accountable for its completion?
notes.back: The role with primary responsibility.
notes.explanation: Delegation to supporting roles is allowed except where the task discussion or Appendix D prohibits it.
notes.evidence: If completion of a task is delegated, the role with primary responsibility for that task remains accountable for task completion.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Chapter 3, Task delegation, PDF p. 43

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-37 Appendix D, how may risk management roles map to people?
notes.back: Several individuals may fill a single role, or one individual may fill several roles.
notes.explanation: Naming and allocation vary between organisations, but the basic functions remain the same.
notes.evidence: multiple individuals filling a single role or one individual filling multiple roles
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, PDF p. 133

notes.front: When one individual is assigned several risk management roles, Special Publication 800-37 says organisations ensure there are no {{c1::conflicts of interest}}.
notes.explanation: The footnote points to Prepare task P-1, where roles are assigned.
notes.evidence: Organizations ensure that there are no conflicts of interest when assigning the same individual to multiple risk management roles.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities (footnote 113), PDF p. 133

notes.front: What does Prepare task P-1 do, and which roles have primary responsibility?
notes.back: It identifies and assigns people to RMF roles; primary responsibility sits with the head of agency, CIO and SAOP.
notes.explanation: Its expected output is documented RMF role assignments.
notes.evidence: TASK P-1 Identify and assign individuals to specific roles associated with security and privacy risk management. Potential Inputs: Organizational security and privacy policies and procedures; organizational charts. Expected Outputs: Documented Risk Management Framework role assignments. Primary Responsibility: Head of Agency; Chief Information Officer; Senior Agency Official for Privacy.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-1, PDF p. 48

notes.front: Which role has primary responsibility for Prepare task P-2, the risk management strategy?
notes.back: The head of agency.
notes.explanation: The expected output is a risk management strategy with a statement of risk tolerance covering security and privacy risk.
notes.evidence: Expected Outputs: Risk management strategy and statement of risk tolerance inclusive of information security and privacy risk. Primary Responsibility: Head of Agency.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-2, PDF p. 48

notes.front: A new agency head wants a written statement of how much security and privacy risk the agency will tolerate, to guide every later risk decision. Which Prepare task produces it?
notes.back: D) P-2, risk management strategy
notes.explanation: P-2 establishes a risk management strategy that includes a determination of risk tolerance.
notes.evidence: TASK P-2 Establish a risk management strategy for the organization that includes a determination of risk tolerance.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-2, PDF p. 48
notes.choices:
A) P-3, organisation-wide risk assessment
B) P-1, risk management roles
C) P-7, continuous monitoring strategy
D) P-2, risk management strategy
notes.choicesExplained: B: P-1 assigns people to roles. C: P-7 sets how control effectiveness is monitored. A: P-3 assesses risk; it does not set tolerance.

notes.front: What does Prepare task P-3 require, and who has primary responsibility?
notes.back: An organisation-wide risk assessment, updated on an ongoing basis; led by the senior accountable official for risk management or risk executive (function), SAISO and SAOP.
notes.explanation: It draws on system-level assessment results, continuous monitoring and strategic risk considerations.
notes.evidence: Primary Responsibility: Senior Accountable Official for Risk Management or Risk Executive (Function); Senior Agency Information Security Officer; Senior Agency Official for Privacy.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.4, Figure 4 (Task P-3), PDF p. 31
uses: senior accountable official for risk management

notes.front: What does optional Prepare task P-4 establish?
notes.back: Organisationally tailored control baselines and/or Cybersecurity Framework Profiles, documented and published.
notes.explanation: Primary responsibility sits with the mission or business owner and the senior accountable official for risk management or risk executive (function).
notes.evidence: TASK P-4 Establish, document, and publish organizationally-tailored control baselines and/or Cybersecurity Framework Profiles.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-4, PDF p. 50

notes.front: What does Prepare task P-5 do, and which roles have primary responsibility?
notes.back: It identifies, documents and publishes organisation-wide controls available for systems to inherit; SAISO and SAOP are primarily responsible.
notes.explanation: Its outputs include a list of common control providers and the controls they offer.
notes.evidence: TASK P-5 Identify, document, and publish organization-wide common controls that are available for inheritance by organizational systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-5, PDF p. 51

notes.front: A department wants its central identity service and data-centre physical protections listed once, so every new system can simply inherit them rather than build its own. Which Prepare task is this?
notes.back: C) P-5
notes.explanation: Identifying and publishing organisation-wide controls for inheritance is task P-5.
notes.evidence: Expected Outputs: List of common control providers and common controls available for inheritance
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-5, PDF p. 51
notes.choices:
A) P-6
B) P-4
C) P-5
D) P-1
notes.choicesExplained: A: P-6 prioritises systems of the same impact level. B: P-4 tailors baselines or CSF Profiles. D: P-1 assigns people to roles.

notes.front: What is the expected output of optional Prepare task P-6?
notes.back: Organisational systems prioritised into low-, moderate- and high-impact subcategories.
notes.explanation: P-6 prioritises systems that share the same impact level; its primary role is the senior accountable official for risk management or risk executive (function).
notes.evidence: Expected Outputs: Organizational systems prioritized into low-, moderate-, and high-impact subcategories.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-6, PDF p. 52
uses: senior accountable official for risk management

notes.front: What does Prepare task P-7 produce, and who has primary responsibility?
notes.back: An implemented organisation-wide strategy for continuously monitoring control effectiveness; the senior accountable official for risk management or risk executive (function).
notes.explanation: Its inputs include the risk management strategy and organisation- and system-level risk assessment results.
notes.evidence: Expected Outputs: An implemented organizational continuous monitoring strategy. Primary Responsibility: Senior Accountable Official for Risk Management or Risk Executive (Function).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-7, PDF p. 53
uses: senior accountable official for risk management

notes.front: A ministry has no common approach to how often its controls are checked; each system team decides for itself. Which Prepare task addresses this gap?
notes.back: D) P-7
notes.explanation: P-7 develops and implements an organisation-wide strategy for continuously monitoring control effectiveness.
notes.evidence: TASK P-7 Develop and implement an organization-wide strategy for continuously monitoring control effectiveness.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-7, PDF p. 53
notes.choices:
A) P-3
B) P-2
C) P-5
D) P-7
notes.choicesExplained: A: P-3 assesses organisation-wide risk. C: P-5 publishes controls for inheritance. B: P-2 sets the risk management strategy and tolerance, not the monitoring strategy.

notes.front: Which Prepare tasks are carried out at the system level in Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: Tasks P-8 to P-18.
notes.explanation: Tasks P-1 to P-7 are the organisation-level set.
notes.evidence: Table 2 provides a summary of tasks and expected outcomes for the RMF Prepare step at the system level.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Table 2, PDF p. 55

notes.front: What does Prepare task P-14 require?
notes.back: A system-level risk assessment, with the results updated on an ongoing basis.
notes.explanation: It mirrors P-3, which does the same for the organisation as a whole.
notes.evidence: TASK P-14 Conduct a system-level risk assessment and update the risk assessment results on an ongoing basis.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-14, PDF p. 60

notes.front: What does Prepare task P-18 do, and who has primary responsibility?
notes.back: It registers the system with organisational programme or management offices; the system owner is primarily responsible.
notes.explanation: Registration informs the governing organisation of the system, its key characteristics and its expected security and privacy implications.
notes.evidence: Expected Outputs: Registered system in accordance with organizational policy. Primary Responsibility: System Owner.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-18, PDF p. 64

notes.front: A research agency plans a new grants system. Before development starts, the programme office needs to know the system is coming, what it is and its expected security and privacy implications. Which task and role cover this?
notes.back: A) P-18, by the system owner
notes.explanation: System registration informs the governing organisation of plans to develop the system; the system owner has primary responsibility.
notes.evidence: System registration, in accordance with organizational policy, serves to inform the governing organization of plans to develop the system or the existence of the system
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 3.1, Task P-18, PDF p. 64
notes.choices:
A) P-18, by the system owner
B) P-2, by the head of agency
C) P-14, by a control assessor
D) P-1, by the CIO
notes.choicesExplained: B: P-2 sets the organisation's risk strategy. C: P-14 is a system-level risk assessment, and assessors do not own it. D: P-1 assigns roles.

notes.front: Special Publication 800-37 calls the authorising official the {{c1::only}} organisational official who can accept the security and privacy risk to operations, assets and individuals.
notes.explanation: AOs sit in management positions with authority to match understanding and accepting such risk.
notes.evidence: The authorizing official is the only organizational official who can accept the security and privacy risk to organizational operations, organizational assets, and individuals.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official, PDF p. 133

notes.front: What do authorising officials typically have, according to Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: Budgetary oversight for the system, or responsibility for the mission or business operations it supports.
notes.explanation: Accordingly, Special Publication 800-37 places AOs in management positions with authority to match understanding and accepting the risk.
notes.evidence: Authorizing officials typically have budgetary oversight for the system or are responsible for the mission and/or business operations supported by the system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official, PDF p. 133

notes.front: For federal agencies, the role of authorising official is an inherent United States Government function and is assigned to {{c1::government personnel only}}.
notes.explanation: So a federal agency cannot give the AO role to a contractor.
notes.evidence: For federal agencies, the role of authorizing official is an inherent U.S. Government function and is assigned to government personnel only.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official, PDF p. 134

notes.front: A federal agency's AO is overloaded and proposes that the contractor running the system should become the AO. What does Special Publication 800-37 say?
notes.back: D) Not allowed: the AO role is assigned to government personnel only
notes.explanation: The AO role is an inherent United States Government function, so it cannot pass to contractor staff.
notes.evidence: For federal agencies, the role of authorizing official is an inherent U.S. Government function and is assigned to government personnel only.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official, PDF p. 134
notes.choices:
A) Allowed, if the contract names the contractor as AO
B) Allowed, if the contractor is also the system owner
C) Allowed for low-impact systems only
D) Not allowed: the AO role is assigned to government personnel only
notes.choicesExplained: A: no contract clause changes an inherent government function. B: being the system owner does not make contractor staff government personnel. C: Special Publication 800-37 makes no impact-level exception.

notes.front: What is the only activity an authorising official cannot delegate to the AODR?
notes.back: The authorisation decision and signing of the associated decision document, which is the acceptance of risk.
notes.explanation: Everything else in the day-to-day execution of the RMF can be delegated.
notes.evidence: The only activity that cannot be delegated by the authorizing official to the designated representative is the authorization decision and signing of the associated authorization decision document (i.e., the acceptance of risk).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official designated representative, PDF p. 134

notes.front: The AO for a customs system is abroad for a month. The AODR has reviewed all the evidence and wants to sign the decision that accepts the system's risk. What should happen?
notes.back: B) The AO must make and sign the decision; the AODR cannot
notes.explanation: Accepting risk through the authorisation decision is the one activity the AO cannot delegate.
notes.evidence: The only activity that cannot be delegated by the authorizing official to the designated representative is the authorization decision
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official designated representative, PDF p. 134
notes.choices:
A) The AODR signs, since it acts on the AO's behalf
B) The AO must make and sign the decision; the AODR cannot
C) The system owner signs in the AO's absence
D) The SAISO signs as the CIO's liaison
notes.choicesExplained: A: acting on the AO's behalf stops short of the decision itself. C: the system owner submits for adjudication; it does not accept risk. D: the SAISO may be an AODR, which still cannot sign.

notes.front: How does the AODR's authority differ from the AO's?
notes.back: The AODR coordinates and conducts day-to-day risk activities for the AO; only the AO makes the authorisation decision and accepts the risk.
notes.explanation: The AO also remains responsible and accountable for authorisation activities delegated to designated representatives.
notes.evidence: Authorizing officials are responsible and accountable for ensuring that authorization activities and functions that are delegated to authorizing official designated representatives are carried out as specified.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Authorizing official, PDF p. 134

notes.front: Besides implementing and monitoring inherited controls, what are two things Special Publication 800-37 makes a common control provider responsible for?
notes.back: Two of: documenting the controls in security and privacy plans; having them assessed by qualified, suitably independent assessors; documenting findings in assessment reports.
notes.explanation: Providers also produce plans of action for controls with deficiencies.
notes.evidence: ensuring that required assessments of the common controls are conducted by qualified assessors with an appropriate level of independence; documenting assessment findings in control assessment reports
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Common control provider, PDF p. 135

notes.front: A university's network team runs the campus firewalls and intrusion detection that every departmental system relies on, and arranges for those protections to be assessed and monitored. What is the team's RMF role?
notes.back: A) Common control provider
notes.explanation: Implementing, assessing and monitoring controls that other systems inherit is the CCP's role.
notes.evidence: The common control provider is an individual, group, or organization that is responsible for the implementation, assessment, and monitoring of common controls
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Common control provider, PDF p. 135
notes.choices:
A) Common control provider
B) System security officer
C) Control assessor
D) Information owner or steward
notes.choicesExplained: C: the team arranges assessments; it does not perform them. B: an SSO looks after one system's posture, not shared controls. D: the team has no authority over specified information.

notes.front: In a system-level control assessment, what does the control assessor not assess?
notes.back: Inherited controls; only the system-implemented portions of hybrid controls are assessed.
notes.explanation: For common controls, the assessor looks at the implemented common controls and the common-control parts of hybrid controls.
notes.evidence: For system-level control assessments, control assessors do not assess inherited controls, and only assess the system-implemented portions of hybrid controls.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Control assessor, PDF p. 136

notes.front: Besides finding deficiencies, what two things can control assessors provide, according to Special Publication 800-37?
notes.back: An assessment of the severity of the deficiencies; and recommended corrective actions.
notes.explanation: Assessors also prepare the security and privacy assessment reports with their results and findings.
notes.evidence: Control assessors provide an assessment of the severity of the deficiencies discovered in the system, environment of operation, and common controls and can recommend corrective actions
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Control assessor, PDF p. 136

notes.front: An agency hires an outside team to test whether a benefits system's implemented controls are working correctly and producing the desired outcome, and to rate the severity of any deficiencies. What RMF role does the team fill?
notes.back: B) Control assessor
notes.explanation: Determining control effectiveness and the severity of deficiencies is the control assessor's job.
notes.evidence: responsible for conducting a comprehensive assessment of implemented controls and control enhancements to determine the effectiveness of the controls
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Control assessor, PDF p. 136
notes.choices:
A) Common control provider
B) Control assessor
C) System owner
D) Authorising official designated representative
notes.choicesExplained: A: a CCP implements shared controls. C: the system owner receives the results. D: an AODR coordinates for the AO; it does not test controls.

notes.front: What other names may organisations use for the senior agency information security officer?
notes.back: Senior information security officer or chief information security officer.
notes.explanation: The SAISO heads an office with the mission and resources to help achieve trustworthy, secure information and systems.
notes.evidence: Organizations may also refer to the senior agency information security officer as the senior information security officer or chief information security officer.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior agency information security officer, PDF p. 141

notes.front: What does the SAOP review and approve before a system is authorised, reauthorised or given ongoing authorisation?
notes.back: The privacy plans for the information systems.
notes.explanation: This is one of several privacy duties Special Publication 800-37 lists for the SAOP.
notes.evidence: Reviewing and approving privacy plans for information systems prior to authorization, reauthorization, or ongoing authorization;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior agency official for privacy, PDF p. 141

notes.front: Who designates which privacy controls may be treated as common controls?
notes.back: The senior agency official for privacy.
notes.explanation: Privacy controls designated as common are documented in the organisation's privacy program plan.
notes.evidence: The senior agency official for privacy is responsible for designating which privacy controls may be treated as common controls.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Common control provider, PDF p. 135

notes.front: A tax agency is about to authorise a new system that collects taxpayers' PII. Which official reviews the categorisation and the privacy plan, and answers agency-wide for privacy risk?
notes.back: C) Senior agency official for privacy
notes.explanation: The SAOP reviews and approves categorisations of systems handling PII and privacy plans before authorisation.
notes.evidence: Reviewing and approving the categorization of information systems that create, collect, use, process, store, maintain, disseminate, disclose, or dispose of personally identifiable information;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior agency official for privacy, PDF p. 141
notes.choices:
A) Senior agency information security officer
B) System security officer
C) Senior agency official for privacy
D) Enterprise architect
notes.choicesExplained: A: the SAISO leads security, and coordinates with the SAOP on privacy. B: an SSO handles one system day to day. D: the enterprise architect places systems in the architecture.

notes.front: How does the SAISO's remit differ from the SAOP's?
notes.back: The SAISO carries out the CIO's security responsibilities; the SAOP answers agency-wide for privacy compliance and privacy risk.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 requires the two to coordinate so the security and privacy programmes work together.
notes.evidence: The senior agency information security officer is also responsible for coordinating with the senior agency official for privacy to ensure coordination between privacy and information security programs.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior agency information security officer, PDF p. 141

notes.front: Who can be the senior accountable official for risk management?
notes.back: The head of the agency, or an individual the head of the agency designates.
notes.explanation: This official may keep the risk executive (function) or delegate it to another official or group.
notes.evidence: The senior accountable official for risk management is the head of the agency or an individual designated by the head of the agency.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Senior accountable official for risk management, PDF p. 140
uses: senior accountable official for risk management

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-37, what role may the CIO be designated for selected systems?
notes.back: Authorising official, or co-authorising official with other senior officials.
notes.explanation: The CIO role is itself an inherent United States Government function, assigned to government personnel only.
notes.evidence: For selected systems, the chief information officer may be designated as an authorizing official or a co-authorizing official with other senior organizational officials.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Chief information officer, PDF p. 135

notes.front: With whom does the system owner decide who has access to the system, and with what privileges?
notes.back: The information owner or steward.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 notes that the decision about access to specific information may rest with the information owner or steward.
notes.evidence: In coordination with the information owner/steward, the system owner decides who has access to the system (and with what types of privileges or access rights).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System owner, PDF p. 142

notes.front: In Special Publication 800-37, what does the system owner develop and maintain in coordination with the system security and privacy officers?
notes.back: The security and privacy plans.
notes.explanation: The system owner also ensures the system operates in line with the selected and implemented controls.
notes.evidence: In coordination with the system security and privacy officers, the system owner is responsible for the development and maintenance of the security and privacy plans
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System owner, PDF p. 142

notes.front: When information is shared with other organisations, what happens to the information owner's responsibility for rules on its use and protection?
notes.back: The information owner or steward retains it.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 says the owner sets the rules for appropriate use and protection in information-sharing environments.
notes.evidence: the information owner/steward is responsible for establishing the rules for appropriate use and protection of the information and retains that responsibility even when the information is shared with or provided to other organizations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Information owner or steward, PDF p. 138

notes.front: How does the information owner or steward differ from the system owner?
notes.back: The information owner has authority over information; the system owner answers for the system across its life. They may or may not be one person.
notes.explanation: A single system may hold information from several information owners.
notes.evidence: The owner/steward of the information processed, stored, or transmitted by a system may or may not be the same individual as the system owner. An individual system may contain information from multiple information owners/stewards.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Information owner or steward, PDF p. 138

notes.front: A national statistics office shares survey microdata with a university. The university asks who sets the rules for how the data may be used and protected. Who is it, in Special Publication 800-37 terms?
notes.back: C) The statistics office's information owner or steward
notes.explanation: The information owner sets rules for use and protection, and keeps that responsibility when the information is shared.
notes.evidence: retains that responsibility even when the information is shared with or provided to other organizations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Information owner or steward, PDF p. 138
notes.choices:
A) The university's system owner
B) The university's system security officer
C) The statistics office's information owner or steward
D) The statistics office's CIO
notes.choicesExplained: A: the receiving system owner runs the system but does not gain authority over the information. B: an SSO keeps a system's posture, not information rules. D: the CIO runs the security programme, not rules for specific information.

notes.front: Special Publication 800-37 says the SSO's day-to-day responsibility may include several areas. What are two of them?
notes.back: Two of: physical and environmental protection; personnel security; incident handling; security and privacy training and awareness.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 frames these as "not limited to", so the list is open.
notes.evidence: This responsibility may also include, but is not limited to, physical and environmental protection; personnel security; incident handling; and security and privacy training and awareness.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System security or privacy officer, PDF p. 143

notes.front: When the system security officer and system privacy officer are separate roles, how are their responsibilities divided?
notes.back: The security officer protects against unauthorised activity to provide confidentiality, integrity and availability; the privacy officer handles privacy compliance and privacy risk from processing PII.
notes.explanation: Their responsibilities overlap where the system protects the security of PII.
notes.evidence: The responsibilities of system security officers and system privacy officers overlap regarding aspects of the system that protect the security of PII.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System security or privacy officer, PDF p. 143

notes.front: On a court records system, one person reviews security alerts each morning, manages and controls changes, updates the security plan and advises the system owner on control issues. What is this person's RMF role?
notes.back: B) System security officer
notes.explanation: Day-to-day security operations and principal advice on the system's controls fall to the SSO, working closely with the system owner.
notes.evidence: The system security or privacy officer also serves as a principal advisor on all matters, technical and otherwise, involving the controls for the system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System security or privacy officer, PDF p. 143
notes.choices:
A) Enterprise architect
B) System security officer
C) Common control provider
D) Mission or business owner
notes.choicesExplained: A: the architect works on the enterprise view, not one system's daily posture. C: a CCP runs controls other systems inherit. D: the mission owner sets needs and requirements; it does not run daily security.

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-37, what may mission or business owners also serve as?
notes.back: Authorising officials.
notes.explanation: They also provide essential inputs to the risk management strategy.
notes.evidence: Mission and business owners provide essential inputs to the risk management strategy, play an active part in the SDLC, and may also serve in the role of authorizing official.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Mission or business owner, PDF p. 138

notes.front: With whom does Special Publication 800-37 say enterprise architects collaborate on boundary determinations and allocating controls to system elements?
notes.back: System owners and authorising officials.
notes.explanation: Enterprise architects also serve as part of the risk executive (function).
notes.evidence: Collaborate with system owners and authorizing officials to facilitate authorization boundary determinations and allocation of controls to system elements;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Enterprise architect, PDF p. 137

notes.front: A newly created agency has no one running its security programme. Whose responsibility is it to designate the senior agency information security officer?
notes.back: A) The chief information officer
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 makes designating the SAISO one of the CIO's responsibilities.
notes.evidence: The chief information officer 117 is an organizational official responsible for designating a senior agency information security officer
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, Chief information officer, PDF p. 134
notes.choices:
A) The chief information officer
B) The authorising official
C) Each system owner
D) The senior agency official for privacy
notes.choicesExplained: C: system owners run individual systems. B: the AO accepts risk for systems; it does not appoint programme officials. D: the SAOP leads privacy and coordinates with the SAISO.

notes.front: A state agency wants one structured but flexible process covering categorisation, control selection, implementation and assessment, authorisations and continuous monitoring of its systems. Which NIST framework matches that description?
notes.back: B) The Risk Management Framework in Special Publication 800-37
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-37 describes the RMF as exactly this disciplined, structured and flexible process.
notes.evidence: The RMF provides a disciplined, structured, and flexible process for managing security and privacy risk that includes information security categorization; control selection, implementation, and assessment; system and common control authorizations; and continuous monitoring.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Abstract, PDF p. 4
notes.choices:
A) The Special Publication 800-30 risk assessment process
B) The Risk Management Framework in Special Publication 800-37
C) A CSF Community Profile
D) An enterprise risk register
notes.choicesExplained: A: Special Publication 800-30 guides risk assessments, one input among many. C: a Community Profile is a shared set of CSF outcomes. D: a risk register records risks; it is not a process.

notes.front: Before categorising any of its systems, a ministry assigns people to risk roles, sets its risk tolerance and publishes controls that systems can inherit. Which RMF step is it in?
notes.back: D) Prepare
notes.explanation: Establishing the context and priorities for managing risk before the main steps is the Prepare step.
notes.evidence: Prepare to execute the RMF from an organization- and a system-level perspective by establishing a context and priorities for managing security and privacy risk.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Section 2.2, RMF steps and structure, PDF p. 27
notes.choices:
A) Categorize
B) Select
C) Monitor
D) Prepare
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing has been categorised yet. B: no controls are being chosen for a system. C: there is no authorised system to monitor.

notes.front: At a transport agency, one manager bought the new rostering system, oversees its operation and maintenance, will arrange its disposal and makes sure its users receive the required security and privacy training. What is this manager's RMF role?
notes.back: B) System owner
notes.explanation: Responsibility from procurement to disposal, including user training, belongs to the system owner.
notes.evidence: The system owner ensures that system users and support personnel receive the requisite security and privacy training.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations, Appendix D, Roles and responsibilities, System owner, PDF p. 142
notes.choices:
A) Information owner or steward
B) System owner
C) Authorising official
D) System security officer
notes.choicesExplained: A: that role has authority over information, not the system's life. C: the AO accepts risk; it does not run the system. D: the SSO maintains security posture day to day, working with the owner.
